# Part VII. Designing Better Decisions {.unnumbered}

The committee knows it should hear independent judgments, yet the most senior member still speaks first. A student plans to study, yet the phone remains beside the keyboard. Knowing the problem has not changed the situation that keeps producing it: reservations go unspoken and study time slips away. What could change in the meeting or at the desk to make the intended action easier?

The route in @fig-part-7-route turns an explanation of the problem into a proposed change and a test of its effects. Behavior design asks what would make a useful action easier to repeat. Choice architecture examines how options are presented and how people move from intention to action. Decision hygiene considers the procedures through which a group gathers evidence, compares judgments, and learns from results.

The final chapter, [Deciding With Data and AI](../chapters/42-data-driven-decision-making.qmd#why-this-final-chapter), brings that work back to the distinction between prediction, valuation, and choice introduced in Chapter 1. An improved prediction still leaves people to decide what matters and which action to take. The earlier questions about evidence, values, and disagreement therefore remain necessary when AI enters the process. Chapter 41 builds a procedure that can be examined and revised; Chapter 42 asks how a tool can improve that procedure and how we would know whether it has.

Each intervention is a proposal to test. We need to identify whose goal it serves, what outcome would count as improvement, and how affected people can question or leave the arrangement.

![Where is the obstacle, what conditions can change, and what do the results show? Part VII turns a diagnosis into a change that can be tested.](../figures/master-loop-part-7.svg){#fig-part-7-route fig-alt="Three reading questions: Where is the obstacle? What conditions can change? What do the results show?" .phone-fit}

## Questions to carry forward

- Where does the intended action break down?
- What small change to the conditions addresses that obstacle?
- What evidence will show improvement, failure, or harm?

We return to the hiring committee with a more useful question than whether its members are rational. How could its next decision be made easier to examine, challenge, and improve?
